strengths: The paper identifies a practically important scaling problem: producing many per-scene NeRF-like representations efficiently rather than optimizing each scene fully independently.
The proposed combination of latent-space rendering with a shared Micro-Macro Tri-Plane decomposition is technically plausible and well motivated for reducing per-scene trainable parameters.
The experiments report substantial reductions in second-stage per-scene training time and storage compared with RGB Tri-Planes, while preserving similar PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS on the two tested datasets.
The ablation study is useful: it separately probes latent-space training, micro-only, macro-only, and the number of shared macro planes, supporting the main design choices.
The paper is generally clear, with equations, an algorithm, and hyperparameter tables that improve reproducibility.
weaknesses: The evaluation is too narrow for the strength of the claims. Results are limited to two synthetic/object-centric datasets at 128x128 resolution, with no real-world scenes, more diverse scene distributions, higher-resolution evaluation, or out-of-distribution analysis.

The strongest baseline comparison is only against independently optimized methods, especially Tri-Planes. The paper does not adequately compare to category-level/shared-prior approaches, learned initializations, amortized reconstruction, hypernetwork/functa-style methods, or other multi-scene representation learning techniques that are highly relevant to the proposed setting.

The novelty is moderate: shared basis/dictionary representations plus per-instance coefficients and latent NeRF training are natural combinations of existing ideas. The paper positions the task well, but the algorithmic contribution feels incremental rather than clearly transformative.

The resource-cost claims need more careful accounting. Stage 1 is expensive and requires 500 scenes; the break-even point, sensitivity to N1, and amortization across different dataset sizes are not sufficiently explored. It is also unclear how fine-tuning shared macro planes in stage 2 affects previously learned stage-1 scenes or stability as more scenes are added.

Quality comparisons are underdeveloped. Main NVS metrics are averaged over only 50 sampled scenes, qualitative examples are limited, and the method is compared for quality mainly to RGB Tri-Planes rather than the broader methods used in the resource figure.

The method assumes all scenes come from a common distribution and benefit from shared macro planes, but the paper does not test mixed categories, heterogeneous scenes, or failure modes when the shared representation is less appropriate.

Some technical details are ambiguous or contain minor inconsistencies, such as notation around the autoencoder reconstruction equation and dataset/figure labeling issues, which slightly weaken confidence in polish and reproducibility.

Ethical and practical considerations are not discussed, though the main risks are limited; still, large-scale 3D reconstruction pipelines can raise dataset provenance and privacy issues in real deployments.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant scaling problem: learning many related scene representations more efficiently is important for NeRF datasets and downstream 3D generative pipelines.
The proposed two-stage pipeline is conceptually simple and plausible, combining latent-space rendering with a shared/per-scene decomposition of Tri-Planes.
Reported per-scene training and storage costs are substantially lower than RGB Tri-Planes after the first stage, while preserving similar PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS on the two evaluated datasets.
The paper includes some useful ablations over micro planes, macro planes, number of shared bases, and latent-space training.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. The work mainly combines known ingredients: Tri-Planes, latent NeRF/IG-AE-style training, and shared basis representations. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish the technical contribution from prior amortized or shared-initialization neural field methods.

The evaluation is too narrow for the strength of the claims. Experiments are only on two synthetic/object-centric datasets at 128x128 resolution, with no real scenes, no high-resolution setting, no diverse scene distributions, and no convincing evidence that the method works beyond tightly aligned categories such as cars and faces.

The baseline comparison is weak. The main quality comparison is essentially against RGB Tri-Planes, and only on 50 sampled scenes due to training cost. The broader resource comparison in the appendix appears shallow and potentially unfair, with methods differing substantially in quality, representation, and likely tuning; some baselines achieve much higher PSNR than the proposed method, undercutting the claim of comparable quality.

The formulation has an important scalability caveat: stage 2 fine-tunes shared macro planes and the decoder while learning new scenes. This can alter previously learned scenes and makes the claimed ability to add scenes cheaply less clean than presented. The paper does not adequately analyze forgetting, ordering effects, or whether old scenes remain stable after adding new ones.

The reported memory and time metrics are ambiguous. It is not always clear whether memory means storage footprint or training memory, how shared components are amortized, and whether comparisons include all model components consistently. The asymptotic framing also hides the dependence on the expensive first stage and on the assumption that future scenes come from the same distribution.

The ablation study is limited and does not fully isolate the contribution of each design choice. It lacks sensitivity to N1, number of scenes, category diversity, latent resolution, number of shared bases, and distribution shift between stage-1 and stage-2 scenes.

Claims are stronger than the evidence. The paper frames the method as a general solution for scaled inverse graphics, but the experiments support a much narrower conclusion: it can compress and accelerate Tri-Plane fitting for related synthetic object collections under a fixed setup.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript. Hyperparameters are listed, but important implementation details, training schedules, exact evaluation protocol, baseline tuning, and code availability are deferred to supplementary/open-source release rather than made sufficiently auditable in the paper.

strengths: The paper identifies a timely and practically important scaling problem for inverse graphics: learning large collections of scene representations, rather than optimizing one scene at a time.

The proposed micro/macro tri-plane decomposition is simple, well-motivated, and well matched to the problem setting: scene-specific micro planes preserve instance detail while shared macro planes amortize common structure across many scenes.

The two-stage training design is coherent and yields large reported efficiency gains. On ShapeNet Cars, the method reduces second-stage per-scene training time from 16.02 minutes to 2.23 minutes and per-scene storage from 1.50 MB to 0.48 MB, while maintaining similar PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS to RGB tri-planes.
The paper includes useful ablations isolating the latent space, micro planes, macro planes, and number of shared base planes, which generally support the main design choices.
The writing is mostly clear, and the method is easy to understand. Hyperparameters and an algorithm are provided, and the authors state that code is available in the supplement and will be released.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is somewhat narrow for the strength of the claims. Evaluation is limited to two synthetic/object-centric datasets at 128x128 resolution, with only 50 randomly sampled scenes used for the main NVS comparison against tri-planes. It is unclear how well the method transfers to more diverse, real, high-resolution, or less category-homogeneous scenes.

The comparison to recent methods in the resource-cost figure/table is not fully convincing. Many baselines target different quality/speed/memory tradeoffs, and the paper does not clearly establish that they were tuned comparably for this scaled setting. The main high-quality comparison is essentially against the tri-plane base representation.

The method relies on a substantial first-stage cost: 31.2 hours and 361 MB for 500 scenes. The break-even point and sensitivity to N1, dataset homogeneity, and the number of macro bases M are not deeply analyzed, even though these determine when the approach is practically beneficial.

There is a potential consistency issue from fine-tuning the shared macro planes B during stage 2: updating B can change the representations of stage-1 scenes that also depend on B. The paper should more explicitly explain whether stage-1 quality is preserved after stage-2 fine-tuning or whether macro components are cached/frozen for earlier scenes.

The novelty is useful but incremental: the approach combines latent NeRF-style training, tri-plane representations, and shared basis/low-rank-style decomposition. The paper would be stronger with more direct positioning against learned initialization, shared latent-code, compression, or amortized NeRF methods.

Some details and presentation issues remain: Figure 4 says ShapeNet Cats while the dataset is ShapeNet Cars; the text says test views are reserved to evaluate tri-planes rather than all methods; and there are minor typos such as 'Strutural' and 'nase planes'. These do not undermine the core idea but slightly reduce polish.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and practical bottleneck: learning large collections of 3D scene representations with lower time and storage cost while preserving a planar structure compatible with image-model pipelines.

The proposed representation is clear: decomposing tri-plane features into scene-specific micro planes and shared macro/base planes is simple, interpretable, and well motivated for multi-scene settings.

Empirical results show substantial efficiency gains over standard Tri-Planes and K-Planes, with Fused-Planes reducing per-scene memory and training time while often improving over Tri-Planes in NVS metrics.

The paper includes a broad set of baselines, reports PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS plus resource costs, and provides useful ablations for latent-space training, micro/macro components, and the number of shared base planes.
The appendix gives implementation details and hyperparameters, and the stated plan to release code improves reproducibility prospects.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate: the method largely combines shared basis representations, tri-plane factorization, and latent-space NeRF training. The key ingredients are plausible but not conceptually deep, and the paper relies heavily on an anonymous prior for the 3D-aware latent-space component.

The experimental setting is narrow: all main evaluations are on synthetic, object-centric, low-resolution 128x128 data. It is unclear whether the approach transfers to real captured scenes, higher resolutions, complex backgrounds, or less category-homogeneous datasets.

The quality-efficiency tradeoff is not uniformly compelling. Fused-Planes is much worse in reconstruction quality than strong single-scene methods such as TensoRF/Vanilla-NeRF on ShapeNet, and SPARF-128 is much faster with comparable or sometimes better quality despite being non-planar.

The evaluation of NVS quality is based on a small sampled subset for many comparisons, reportedly 16 ShapeNet scenes and 4 Basel Faces scenes, which weakens confidence in the quantitative claims for large-scale multi-scene learning.

The resource accounting is somewhat hard to interpret. Table 1 reports per-scene costs while the method has a two-stage training regime with shared components, and the comparison depends strongly on amortization assumptions over N scenes.

A potentially important issue is that shared base planes and the decoder are fine-tuned while learning the second subset. This can change the representation of previously learned scenes, but the paper does not deeply analyze forgetting, stability, or what happens when scenes are added incrementally after deployment.

The paper motivates planar compatibility with downstream 2D/image-model pipelines, but does not demonstrate a downstream use case such as generative modeling, feed-forward reconstruction, or diffusion over the learned planar representations.
Some claims are overstated, e.g. calling the work a pivotal milestone, given the limited datasets, moderate novelty, and remaining gap to stronger non-planar or single-scene methods.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant efficiency problem for training many 3D scene representations, and the framing around per-scene training time and memory is useful for this setting.

The proposed micro/macro decomposition is simple and reasonably motivated: shared base planes can amortize common structure while retaining a planar representation compatible with 2D-style processing.

The paper includes several baselines across single-scene and many-scene methods, reports time and memory in addition to PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS, and provides ablations for latent-space training, shared macro planes, and the number of base planes.
The method appears to give meaningful resource savings over the Tri-Planes baseline while improving its reconstruction metrics in the reported setting.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. The method largely combines Tri-Planes, a low-rank/shared-basis style decomposition, and a 3D-aware latent-space training pipeline from a prior anonymous work. The paper does not convincingly isolate what is conceptually new beyond this engineering combination.

The empirical support is much weaker than the broad claims. Main NVS quality comparisons are averaged over only 16 ShapeNet scenes and 4 Basel Face scenes, despite the paper claiming large-set learning over thousands of scenes. This small evaluation sample makes the reported quality comparisons and rankings fragile.

The evaluation is confined to synthetic, low-resolution 128x128 object/face datasets. This is a narrow setting for claims about large-scale multi-scene inverse graphics, product inventories, VR assets, or general 3D reconstruction workflows.

The method does not actually establish state-of-the-art overall performance: several standard single-scene methods have substantially better NVS quality, and SPARF-128 is faster and often competitive or better. The paper narrows the claim to planar representations, but the title and conclusion overstate the significance.

Resource accounting is not fully convincing. The method depends on training or fine-tuning shared components and a VAE initialized from Stable Diffusion, yet the comparison focuses on simplified per-scene coefficients. It is unclear whether all pretraining, tuning, shared-component storage, and implementation differences are fairly accounted for across methods.

Baseline fairness is questionable. Many baselines are taken from Nerfstudio implementations, but the paper gives little evidence that each was tuned comparably for these small synthetic scenes and low-resolution renders. The adapted CodeNeRF baseline is introduced by the authors, but its competitiveness and implementation fidelity are not well validated.

The ablations are incomplete. They show small metric changes but do not examine sensitivity to the number of first-stage scenes, number of base planes beyond one setting, latent dimension/resolution, category transfer, scene diversity, or whether the learned bases generalize to genuinely new distributions.

The central multi-scene claim would be stronger with downstream evidence, such as training a generative model or feed-forward reconstruction model on the learned representations. As written, the paper mostly evaluates storage/training cost and NVS metrics, not whether the representation preserves the practical advantages claimed for planar methods.

The paper has reproducibility and clarity issues: the project page appears blank in the extracted manuscript, one key dependency is cited as Anonymous (2025), and there are notation/typographical issues such as the autoencoder reconstruction equation using Dψ(Eψ(x)) instead of Dψ(Eϕ(x)).
The conclusion is overstated, calling the work a pivotal milestone despite relatively modest empirical gains, narrow datasets, and unresolved questions about fairness and generality.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and practically relevant bottleneck: learning large collections of 3D scene representations while retaining the planar structure that makes Tri-Planes useful for downstream 2D-model interoperability.

The proposed micro/macro decomposition is simple, well motivated, and effective: sharing learned base planes across scenes substantially reduces per-scene memory while preserving the planar representation interface.

The empirical results are encouraging. Fused-Planes gives large efficiency gains over Tri-Planes and K-Planes, with much better training time and memory, while maintaining or improving NVS quality relative to Tri-Planes in the reported setting.

The paper includes a broad set of baselines spanning single-scene, many-scene, planar, and non-planar methods, and the ablations support the value of the latent-space training, multiple shared base planes, and micro/macro split.
The presentation is generally clear, with useful scaling analysis, per-scene appendix tables, qualitative comparisons, and hyperparameter details that improve reproducibility.
weaknesses: The evaluation is still somewhat narrow for the strength of the claims. All experiments are on synthetic/object-centric or controlled face data at 128x128 resolution; there is no real-world multi-scene dataset, higher-resolution study, or downstream generative/reconstruction experiment demonstrating that the retained planar structure actually benefits later pipelines.

The main NVS comparison is computed on only 4 evaluation scenes per ShapeNet category and 4 Basel Faces scenes, despite training on thousands of scenes. Appendix subset comparisons use 50 scenes for only Cars and Faces, but the headline quantitative claims would be stronger with evaluation over many more held-out scenes and confidence intervals.

The method relies heavily on a 3D-aware latent space from an Anonymous 2025 prior work and a Stable Diffusion VAE initialization. This makes the novelty somewhat entangled with an external unpublished component, and the paper does not sufficiently isolate how much of the efficiency/quality tradeoff comes from Fused-Planes versus the latent-space machinery.

The quality-efficiency tradeoff is favorable only under a specific framing. Compared with strong non-planar single-scene methods, Fused-Planes has lower reconstruction quality; compared with SPARF-128 it is slower and has mixed quality/resource advantages. The main contribution is strongest for planar MSIG, but the paper sometimes phrases the impact more broadly.

The training protocol is relatively complex, with a first subset, warm-up, latent supervision, RGB alignment, shared base fine-tuning, and decoder fine-tuning. The paper gives hyperparameters, but does not fully analyze sensitivity to N1, M, dataset diversity, latent dimension/resolution, or whether shared planes degrade when adding new scenes sequentially.

Some claims about open-source availability and project page are incomplete in the manuscript text, and the abstract appears to have a dangling project-page sentence. There are also minor notation/typo issues such as Dψ(Eψ(x)) where the encoder should likely be Eϕ, and small spelling errors in the appendix.
